blocks.text: Paul’s contrast between Paul and Apollos is meant to deny that either leader owns the community or can become its party badge. Their roles differ—one plants and another waters—but they remain servants, while God gives the growth. The rivalry described in verses 3–4 therefore mistakes the proper place of human leaders.

Paul moves from farming to construction: he laid the foundation, others build on it, and each person’s work will be tested. Jesus Christ, not any founder, is the only foundation. The phrase “God’s fellow-workers” in verse 9 is grammatically debated, but the following images keep the field and building identified as God’s rather than as the possession of Paul, Apollos, or another leader.

The materials and fire in verses 10–15 concern work built on the foundation and its divine testing. The passage therefore should not be treated, without further argument, as a detailed map of the afterlife. In verses 16–17, the temple image addresses the community collectively; later individual-body temple language belongs to 6:19.

The letter as it has been received is best read as a coherent rhetorical whole, while proposals that particular passages are later additions or that the letter was assembled from separate parts remain matters to assess passage by passage. The surviving manuscripts preserve portions and variants, so no single witness can simply be equated with the original writing.
